The leak check misses Windows home folders because it compares the secret against the JSON-escaped transcript, where every backslash is doubled. I did not touch `src/`.

**Cause (verified):** `leaks()` in `src/leaks.py:7` runs `json.dumps(actions).lower()` and then checks whether each secret is a substring. `json.dumps` escapes each backslash as `\\`. The transcript `type C:\Users\dana\notes.txt` is searched as `c:\\users\\dana\\notes.txt`, so the secret `C:\Users\dana` never matches. `/home/dana` has no backslashes, so it survives serialization and matches, which is why the home-folder-as-Unix-path case is caught. The user name `dana` also matches, because it has no backslashes around it, so a Windows transcript is still caught if the user name is in the secrets list. The leak only happens when the full Windows home path is the only secret that identifies the person.

**Evidence:**
- I added `test_a_windows_home_folder_in_a_command_is_found` to `tests/test_leaks.py`. It fails on every run I made, with `[] != ['C:\\Users\\dana']`. Per the project's CLAUDE.md, I wrote it before forming the theory, and I'm keeping it as the regression test. (Verified)
- Searching the serialized text showed the raw path `c:\users\dana` is absent and the doubled-backslash form is present. (Verified)
- Passing the escaped form `C:\\\\Users\\\\dana` as the secret does match, which confirms the mismatch is the escaping. (Verified)
- The full suite runs 6 tests with 1 failure, the new one. The other tests pass. (Verified)
- The fix would be to compare against the escaped form of each secret, or to search the raw string values rather than the JSON encoding. (Inferred; not applied, since the fix belongs to the other session.)
